Wealthy Parents Are Spending a Fortune to Keep Their Adult Kids Coming Home
 
Plus, America’s richest retiree market and a $450,000 guesthouse for Grandma
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
CHET STRANGE FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

A stocked fridge and my childhood bed were always enough to get me home. But some homeowners are taking it a step further, building out over-the-top amenities like wellness spas, arcades and bowling lanes to draw their teenage and adult children back to the nest.

 

The hope is that features like golf simulators, juice bars, vending machines and dance studios—often costing hundreds of thousands of dollars—will encourage more family time. So far, many are experiencing mixed results.

 

“You can’t force your adult children to visit, but you can make home a very easy place to say yes to,” said interior designer Kristen Kinsella of Soucie Horner Design Collective in Chicago. Her clients have requested karaoke rooms and wellness centers for their children with $300,000 budgets, she said.

 
 
CHET STRANGE FOR WSJ
 

Seniors in the North Port-Sarasota-Bradenton area are sitting on more than $100 billion in home equity, making it America’s wealthiest retiree real-estate market. Buyers descend on this area for housing variety, from golf communities and age-qualified enclaves to canal-front single-family homes and master-planned developments equipped for age-in-place living, said Nikki Taylor, a Douglas Elliman real-estate agent.

 

Finally, a $450,000 guesthouse upgrade transformed a neglected 600-square-foot space into a showpiece cottage with a slate roof, copper gutters and an arched Dutch door.

 
 
 

The Parents Building Bowling Alleys and Wellness Spas to Keep Their Kids Home

 
 
CHET STRANGE FOR WSJ
 

Wealthy homeowners are pouring millions into pricey perks for their older children, but even arcades and pickleball courts don’t always keep them around.

They Turned a Neglected Guesthouse Into a $450,000 Cottage for Grandma

 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

What started as a simple dishwasher upgrade evolved into a full-scale transformation centered on family and food.

 
 
 

What’s the Deal?

 
 
ERIC PHILLIPS
 

Model Bella Hadid has purchased a house in Crested Butte, Colo., for $5.5 million. The home was built in 2001 around two old coal-miner’s sheds dating back to the early 1900s.

 

A waterfront compound in Palm Beach, Fla., with a dock on the Intracoastal Waterway has sold in an off-market deal. Billionaire Netscape co-founder Jim Clark and his wife, Kristy Hinze Clark, purchased the property for $84 million plus furniture and art for almost $100 million in total.

 

A Tuscan-inspired Aspen, Colo., mansion owned by Australian billionaire James Packer and his ex-wife, Erica Parker, has sold for $42.68 million. The sale comes amid a slowdown in the tony Colorado ski destination’s high-end market.

After seeing Johnny Depp’s band perform, Nicolas Cage struck up a friendship with him. “Six months later, Nic suggested I try acting. I was up for anything that would help pay the bills.”

 
 
 

House of the Week

 
 
DAVID HEATH
 

WSJ’s House of the Week takes readers five stories above ground in North Georgia.

 

A retired landscaper and real-estate investor spent three years planning and designing a metal “watchtower” made of two repurposed shipping containers. One pod houses a bedroom, kitchenette, and dining area, while the other contains a bathroom and utilities.
